cards.q: What does it mean to say that alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons?
cards.a: Saturated: only single C–C bonds (no C=C). Hydrocarbon: made of carbon and hydrogen only.
cards.why: Every carbon has the maximum number of atoms bonded to it, so alkanes cannot take part in addition reactions.

cards.q: An alkane has \(M_{\text{r}} = 86.0\). Find its molecular formula. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0)
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{14}}\)
steps: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{14}}\): hexane or one of its isomers.
cards.why: Each extra CH<sub>2</sub> adds 14 to the relative molecular mass.

cards.q: Give the general formula of the alkanes and of the cycloalkanes.
cards.a: Alkanes \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}\); cycloalkanes \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}\).

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of cyclohexane, a six-membered ring of carbon atoms joined by single bonds.

cards.why: Closing the ring uses one C–C bond in place of two C–H bonds, so a cycloalkane has two fewer H atoms. It is still saturated.

cards.q: What is crude oil (petroleum)?
cards.a: A mixture consisting mainly of alkane hydrocarbons of different chain lengths.
cards.why: It is a finite, non-renewable resource that must be separated into fractions before use.

cards.q: Explain how crude oil is separated by fractional distillation.
cards.a: Fractions separate by boiling point in a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top.
marks: Crude oil is heated so that it vaporises (most of it).
The vapour enters a column with a temperature gradient: hottest at the bottom, coolest at the top.
Vapours rise and each condenses at the level where the temperature falls below its boiling point.
Longer-chain alkanes (higher boiling points) condense lower down; short chains rise higher or leave as gases.
Each fraction is a mixture of alkanes with similar boiling points.

cards.q: Explain why the boiling points of alkanes increase with chain length.
cards.a: Longer chains have stronger van der Waals forces between molecules.
marks: Longer molecules have more electrons and a larger surface area of contact.
So the induced dipole–dipole (van der Waals) forces between molecules are stronger.
More energy is needed to overcome them, so the boiling point is higher.

cards.q: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are isomers. Explain why pentane has the higher boiling point.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of pentane, a straight five-carbon chain, and its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane, a compact, nearly spherical molecule with one carbon joined to four others.

cards.a: Branching reduces the surface contact between molecules.
marks: Both have the same number of electrons.
Pentane molecules are long and can lie close together, with a large area of contact.
2,2-dimethylpropane molecules are compact and nearly spherical, with less contact.
So the van der Waals forces between pentane molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome.

cards.q: Which fraction from crude oil is bottled as cooking gas (LPG) in many homes in West Africa, and what does it contain?
cards.a: The refinery gases fraction: mainly propane and butane.
cards.why: Propane, \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}}\), and butane, \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\), have the lowest boiling points, so they leave at the top of the column.

cards.q: What is cracking?
cards.a: Breaking C–C bonds in long-chain alkanes to form shorter-chain alkanes and alkenes.
cards.why: Cracking turns low-demand heavy fractions into more useful, higher-demand products.

cards.q: Explain the economic reasons for cracking alkanes.
cards.a: Cracking turns surplus long-chain fractions into products that are in demand and worth more.
marks: Fractional distillation gives more of the long-chain fractions than are needed.
There is greater demand for shorter-chain fractions such as petrol than crude oil supplies.
Cracking converts the surplus long chains into shorter, more valuable alkanes (motor fuels).
It also produces alkenes, which are valuable feedstock for polymers and other chemicals.

cards.q: Give the conditions for thermal cracking and its main type of product.
cards.a: High temperature and high pressure. It produces a high percentage of alkenes.
cards.why: Typical conditions are up to about 900 °C and up to about 7000 kPa. The mechanism is not required.

cards.q: Give the conditions for catalytic cracking and its main products.
cards.a: Slight pressure, high temperature and a zeolite catalyst. It produces mainly motor fuels and aromatic hydrocarbons.
cards.why: The catalyst lets cracking happen at a lower temperature and pressure than thermal cracking, saving energy costs. The mechanism is not required.

cards.q: Compare thermal and catalytic cracking: conditions and products.
cards.a:
Thermal: high pressure, high temperature; mainly alkenes.
Catalytic: slight pressure, high temperature, zeolite catalyst; mainly motor fuels (branched alkanes) and aromatic hydrocarbons.
cards.why: Which process is used depends on whether alkenes (for polymers) or petrol is wanted.

cards.q: Write an equation for the cracking of decane into octane and ethene.
cards.why: Check that the carbon and hydrogen atoms balance: 10 C and 22 H on each side.

cards.q: Dodecane, \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{26}}\), is cracked to give octane and ethene only. Write the equation.
cards.why: Missing-product questions are solved by subtracting atoms, then matching a general formula.

cards.q: Explain why cracking an alkane into two products always gives at least one alkene.
cards.a: There are not enough hydrogen atoms for both products to be alkanes.
marks: The alkane has the formula \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}\).
Two alkanes \(\mathrm{C_{a}H_{2a+2}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{b}H_{2b+2}}\) with \(a + b = n\) would need \(2n + 4\) hydrogens.
Only 2n + 2 are available, so at least one product must have fewer hydrogens: an alkene.

cards.q: This scheme shows thermal cracking of hexane. Name the products and explain why the reaction is useful.

figure.alt: Hexane is cracked at high temperature and pressure into butane and ethene.

cards.a: Butane and ethene. Ethene is the feedstock for poly(ethene) and many other chemicals.

cards.q: What is reforming?
cards.a: Processing straight-chain hydrocarbons into branched-chain alkanes and cyclic hydrocarbons.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, a highly branched eight-carbon alkane used as a standard for good-quality petrol.

cards.why: Branched and cyclic hydrocarbons burn more efficiently in engines, so reforming improves petrol. 2,2,4-trimethylpentane is an example.

cards.q: Name the type of process shown and the products.

figure.alt: Hexane is converted into cyclohexane and hydrogen.

cards.a: Reforming: hexane gives cyclohexane and hydrogen.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{14} \rightarrow C_{6}H_{12} + H_{2}}\). The cyclic product burns more efficiently in a petrol engine.

cards.q: Hexane can be reformed into a branched isomer. Draw one possible product.
cards.a: 2-methylpentane (or 3-methylpentane, 2,2- or 2,3-dimethylbutane).

answerFigure.alt: Hexane, a straight six-carbon chain, is reformed into its branched isomer 2-methylpentane.

cards.why: Same molecular formula, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>: only the arrangement of the chain changes.

cards.q: Write an equation for the complete combustion of octane.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{8}H_{18} + 12\tfrac{1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 8CO_{2} + 9H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Or doubled: \(\mathrm{2C_{8}H_{18} + 25O_{2} \rightarrow 16CO_{2} + 18H_{2}O}\). Complete combustion gives only carbon dioxide and water.

cards.q: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of butane, \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\), the main gas in many LPG cylinders.
steps: Carbon: 4 C gives \(\mathrm{4CO_{2}}\). Hydrogen: 10 H gives \(\mathrm{5H_{2}O}\).
Double everything to clear the half.
cards.why: Balance C, then H, then O last, because O<sub>2</sub> appears on its own.

cards.q: Write equations for the incomplete combustion of methane forming (a) carbon monoxide and (b) carbon.
cards.a:
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_{4} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow CO + 2H_{2}O}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_{4} + O_{2} \rightarrow C + 2H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Incomplete combustion happens when the oxygen supply is limited; less energy is released.

cards.q: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed when 1.00 kg of octane, \(\mathrm{C_{8}H_{18}}\), burns completely. (\(M_{\text{r}}\): octane 114.0, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) 44.0)
cards.a: 3.09 kg
cards.why: Burning a fuel makes a greater mass of CO<sub>2</sub> than the fuel itself, because oxygen from the air is added.

cards.q: Name the pollutants produced by the internal combustion engine.
cards.a: Carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen (\(\mathrm{NO_{x}}\)), carbon particulates and unburned hydrocarbons; also sulfur dioxide if the fuel contains sulfur.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide and water are products of complete combustion, not usually listed as these pollutants.

cards.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
cards.a: It stops the blood carrying oxygen.
marks: Carbon monoxide binds strongly to haemoglobin in red blood cells.
This prevents haemoglobin from carrying oxygen around the body.
It is colourless and odourless, so it is not noticed: a danger from charcoal stoves or generators run indoors.

cards.q: Explain how nitrogen monoxide forms in a car engine, with an equation.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{N_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2NO}\)
marks: Nitrogen and oxygen from the air are both drawn into the engine.
The high temperature of the spark and combustion provides enough energy to break the strong N≡N triple bond.
Nitrogen reacts with oxygen: \(\mathrm{N_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2NO}\).

cards.q: Why are oxides of nitrogen a problem in the atmosphere?
cards.a: They are acidic: \(\mathrm{NO}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\), which reacts with water and oxygen to form nitric acid, causing acid rain.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{2NO + O_{2} \rightarrow 2NO_{2}}\), then \(\mathrm{4NO_{2} + O_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 4HNO_{3}}\). NOx also helps form photochemical smog.

cards.q: How does sulfur dioxide form when fuels burn, and why is it a problem?
cards.a: Sulfur impurities in the fuel burn: \(\mathrm{S + O_{2} \rightarrow SO_{2}}\). \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) is an acidic oxide that dissolves in rainwater to cause acid rain.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{SO_{2} + H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}SO_{3}}\); further oxidation gives sulfuric acid. Acid rain damages limestone buildings, trees and aquatic life.

cards.q: What problems are caused by carbon particulates and unburned hydrocarbons?
cards.a: Carbon particulates (soot) damage the lungs and can cause global dimming. Unburned hydrocarbons, with oxides of nitrogen, form photochemical smog.
cards.why: Both come from incomplete combustion, so they are worst in poorly maintained or cold engines.

cards.q: Describe the structure of a catalytic converter and explain why it is built this way.
cards.a: A ceramic honeycomb coated with a thin layer of metal catalysts such as platinum, palladium and rhodium.
cards.why: The honeycomb gives a very large surface area for the gases to react, while using as little of the expensive metal as possible.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction between carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide in a catalytic converter.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2CO + 2NO \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + N_{2}}\)
cards.why: Two toxic gases become carbon dioxide and nitrogen, which is already 78% of the air.

cards.q: In a catalytic converter, unburned octane reacts with nitrogen monoxide to form carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water. Write a balanced equation.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{8}H_{18} + 25NO \rightarrow 8CO_{2} + 12\tfrac{1}{2}N_{2} + 9H_{2}O}\)
steps: O atoms needed on the right: \(16 + 9 = 25\), all from NO, so \(\mathrm{25NO}\).
cards.why: Here NO is the oxidising agent: it supplies the oxygen and is itself reduced to N<sub>2</sub>.

cards.q: True or false: a catalytic converter removes carbon dioxide from car exhaust.
cards.a: False. It turns CO, NO and unburned hydrocarbons into CO2, N2 and H2O, so it increases CO2 output.
cards.why: It solves the problems of toxic and acidic gases, not the greenhouse effect.

cards.q: Explain why sulfur dioxide can be removed from power-station flue gases using calcium oxide or calcium carbonate.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) is acidic; CaO and \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) are basic, so they neutralise it.
marks: Sulfur dioxide is an acidic oxide.
Calcium oxide and calcium carbonate are bases.
\(\mathrm{CaO + SO_{2} \rightarrow CaSO_{3}}\)
\(\mathrm{CaCO_{3} + SO_{2} \rightarrow CaSO_{3} + CO_{2}}\)

cards.q: Flue gas desulfurisation with calcium carbonate releases carbon dioxide. Why is it still used?
cards.a: It prevents \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) causing acid rain, and the product can be oxidised to calcium sulfate (gypsum) and sold, e.g. for plasterboard.
cards.why: Calcium carbonate (limestone) is cheap, and an unwanted pollutant is turned into a useful material.

cards.q: Why are fossil fuels described as non-renewable?
cards.a: They took millions of years to form, so they are being used up much faster than they can be replaced.
cards.why: Crude oil, coal and natural gas are all finite resources.

cards.q: What are biodiesel and bioethanol, and where do they come from?
cards.a: Fuels made from plants. Bioethanol is made by fermenting sugars (e.g. from sugar cane or maize); biodiesel is made from plant oils such as palm oil or rapeseed oil.
cards.why: Both are renewable: the crops can be grown again each season.

cards.q: Bioethanol is sometimes called "carbon neutral". Evaluate this claim.
cards.a: In principle yes, but energy used in growing and processing means it is not completely neutral.
marks: The plants absorb carbon dioxide by photosynthesis as they grow.
Burning the fuel releases the same amount of carbon dioxide back.
But fossil fuels are used for farm machinery, fertilisers, transport and distillation, releasing extra CO<sub>2</sub>.
So the fuel is not completely carbon neutral, though net emissions are lower than for fossil fuels.

cards.q: Give two disadvantages of growing crops for biofuels instead of using fossil fuels.
cards.a: Land used for fuel crops cannot grow food, which can raise food prices; forests may be cleared to make space, destroying habitats and releasing carbon.
cards.why: Large areas of land are needed to replace even part of the fossil fuel used.

cards.q: Write the equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH + 3O_{2} \rightarrow 2CO_{2} + 3H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Remember the oxygen already in the ethanol molecule when balancing the O atoms.

cards.q: What is homolytic fission? What does this diagram show?

figure.alt: Homolytic fission: in UV light the Cl–Cl bond breaks evenly, one electron going to each chlorine atom (two fish-hook arrows), giving two chlorine radicals.

cards.a: Homolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks so that each atom keeps one electron, forming two radicals. Here UV light breaks Cl–Cl into two chlorine radicals.
cards.why: Each fish-hook arrow shows one electron moving. Fish-hook arrows are not required in exam answers for this mechanism.

cards.q: Where is the dot placed in the methyl radical, and why?

figure.alt: Displayed formula of the methyl radical: a carbon with three C–H bonds and a single dot on the carbon for its unpaired electron.

cards.a: On the carbon atom: \(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{3}}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_{3}\bullet}\).
cards.why: The carbon has only three bonds and one unpaired electron; the hydrogens each have a full bonding pair.

cards.q: Give the overall equation and the condition for the reaction of methane with chlorine to form chloromethane.

figure.alt: Methane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light to give chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{4} + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl + HCl}\), in ultraviolet light.
cards.why: Free-radical substitution: a hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom.

cards.q: Write the initiation step for the reaction of methane with chlorine.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} \rightarrow 2Cl\bullet}\)
cards.why: UV light provides the energy for homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, the weakest bond present.

cards.q: Write the two propagation steps for the formation of chloromethane from methane.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cl\bullet + CH_{4} \rightarrow \bullet CH_{3} + HCl}\)
\(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{3} + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl + Cl\bullet}\)
cards.why: Each propagation step uses one radical and makes another, so the overall reaction is a chain reaction.

cards.q: Which step of free-radical substitution is shown, and what is formed?

figure.alt: First propagation step, displayed: a chlorine radical takes a hydrogen atom from methane, forming hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical, whose unpaired electron is on the carbon.

cards.a: The first propagation step: a chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from methane, forming HCl and a methyl radical.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet + CH_{4} \rightarrow \bullet CH_{3} + HCl}\)

cards.q: Which step is shown here, and why does it allow the reaction to continue?

figure.alt: Second propagation step, displayed: a methyl radical reacts with a chlorine molecule, forming chloromethane and a new chlorine radical.

cards.a: The second propagation step. A chlorine radical is regenerated, which can react with another methane molecule.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{3} + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl + Cl\bullet}\). One initiation can lead to thousands of propagation cycles.

cards.q: Write three possible termination steps in the chlorination of methane.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2Cl\bullet \rightarrow Cl_{2}}\)
\(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{3} + Cl\bullet \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl}\)
\(\mathrm{2\bullet CH_{3} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{6}}\)
cards.why: In termination two radicals join, removing radicals from the reaction.

cards.q: Small amounts of ethane are found among the products of the chlorination of methane. Explain using this diagram.

figure.alt: Termination, displayed: two methyl radicals, each with an unpaired electron on carbon, join to form ethane.

cards.a: In a termination step two methyl radicals join to form ethane.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{2\bullet CH_{3} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{6}}\). Termination steps can give products with longer carbon chains.

cards.q: In a free-radical mechanism, what happens in initiation, propagation and termination?
cards.a:
Initiation: radicals are formed.
Propagation: a radical reacts with a molecule, making a product and a new radical.
Termination: two radicals join, removing radicals.
cards.why: Count radicals: initiation increases them, propagation keeps the number the same, termination decreases them.

cards.q: True or false: the first propagation step is \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet + CH_{4} \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl + H\bullet}\).
cards.a: False. The chlorine radical takes a hydrogen atom: \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet + CH_{4} \rightarrow \bullet CH_{3} + HCl}\).
cards.why: Hydrogen radicals are not formed in this mechanism.

cards.q: Dichloromethane also forms when methane reacts with chlorine. What is happening in this step?

figure.alt: Further substitution, displayed: a chlorine radical takes a hydrogen atom from chloromethane, forming hydrogen chloride and a chloromethyl radical, CH2Cl, with its unpaired electron on carbon.

cards.a: Further substitution: a chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from chloromethane, giving a radical that can react with chlorine again.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet + CH_{3}Cl \rightarrow \bullet CH_{2}Cl + HCl}\), then \(\mathrm{\bullet CH_{2}Cl + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{2}Cl_{2} + Cl\bullet}\).

cards.q: Write an overall equation for the formation of tetrachloromethane from methane.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{4} + 4Cl_{2} \rightarrow CCl_{4} + 4HCl}\)
cards.why: Each hydrogen in turn can be replaced by chlorine, giving a mixture of chlorinated products.

cards.q: How can the conditions be chosen to make chloromethane the main product rather than more highly chlorinated compounds?
cards.a: Use excess methane.
cards.why: A chlorine radical is then much more likely to collide with a methane molecule than with chloromethane.

cards.q: Explain why free-radical substitution is of limited use for making a single halogenoalkane.
cards.a: It gives a mixture of products that must be separated, so the yield of any one is low.
marks: Further substitution can replace more than one hydrogen, giving di-, tri- and tetra-substituted products.
Substitution can occur at different positions along the chain, giving position isomers.
Termination steps produce other products, such as longer-chain alkanes.
The products must be separated, and the yield of the wanted product is low.

cards.q: Propane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Draw the two possible monochlorinated products.
cards.a: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of the two monochlorinated products of propane: 1-chloropropane, with Cl on the end carbon, and 2-chloropropane, with Cl on the middle carbon.

cards.why: A chlorine radical can remove a hydrogen from an end carbon or from the middle carbon, so substitution occurs at different positions.

cards.q: Ethane reacts with bromine in UV light. Give the overall equation and the initiation step.

figure.alt: Initiation: in UV light the Br–Br bond breaks homolytically, giving two bromine radicals, each with one unpaired electron.

cards.a:
Overall: \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6} + Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}Br + HBr}\).
Initiation: \(\mathrm{Br_{2} \rightarrow 2Br\bullet}\).
cards.why: Other halogens react by the same mechanism of initiation, propagation and termination.

cards.q: Write the two propagation steps for the reaction of ethane with bromine.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Br\bullet + C_{2}H_{6} \rightarrow \bullet C_{2}H_{5} + HBr}\)
\(\mathrm{\bullet C_{2}H_{5} + Br_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}Br + Br\bullet}\)

answerFigure.alt: Overall, ethane and bromine give bromoethane and hydrogen bromide in UV light.

cards.why: Add the two propagation steps and the radicals cancel to give the overall equation.

cards.q: A trace of butane is found after ethane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Write the step that forms it.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2\bullet C_{2}H_{5} \rightarrow C_{4}H_{10}}\)
cards.why: A termination step in which two ethyl radicals join: another reason the product mixture is hard to purify.

cards.q: Explain why the reaction of methane with chlorine does not happen in the dark at room temperature, but does in UV light.
cards.a: UV light provides the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond and form radicals.
marks: Alkanes are unreactive because C–H and C–C bonds are strong and non-polar.
A radical is needed to start the reaction.
UV light has enough energy to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically, forming chlorine radicals.
Cl–Cl is weaker than the C–H bond, so it is the bond broken in initiation.
